open_obligations: Note that the result is correlational.
Check which tasks Goel et al. use and whether they are drawn from Burns et al.'s NLP datasets.
Check the effect with alternative similarity metrics, which Goel et al. say also hold.
Check which weak and strong models Goel et al. use and how they compare with Burns et al.'s models.
in.other_title: Weak-to-strong gain is larger when weak supervisor and strong student are less similar
in.rationale: Burns et al. ask how different kinds of weak label errors affect generalisation. Goel et al. report that, controlling for the accuracy gap, weak-strong similarity is inversely correlated with weak-to-strong gain (r = -0.35, p < 0.01), so tasks where supervisor and student make less correlated errors tend to yield greater improvements.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how the kind of weak-label errors affects weak-to-strong gains

open_obligations: Note that ICM uses no weak labels, so the setting differs from Burns et al.'s.
Check whether a weak supervisor could elicit the sun concept where ICM cannot.
Note salience is inferred from failure rather than measured.
in.other_title: Unsupervised elicitation fails when the target concept is not salient (sun-poem task)
in.rationale: Burns et al. ask what makes a concept easy or hard to elicit and how to define salience. Wen et al. report ICM performs at chance on a 'poems mentioning sun are better' task with Llama 70B and attribute this to the concept not being salient; ICM is unsupervised elicitation, not weak-to-strong finetuning, and salience is not formally defined.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: what makes a concept hard to elicit without strong supervision, tested with a deliberately non-salient preference

open_obligations: Check whether the theory's assumptions about the pseudolabeler match the weak supervisors Burns et al. use.
Check which datasets and teachers the experiments use.
Check whether the theory explains Burns et al.'s poor reward-modeling results.
in.other_title: Expansion bounds for weak-to-strong: pseudolabel correction and coverage expansion
in.rationale: Burns et al. ask how important errors in the weak supervision are and how different kinds of weak label biases affect generalisation. Lang, Sontag and Vijayaraghavan give error bounds based on expansion of the data distribution and student hypothesis class that capture pseudolabel correction and coverage expansion; they show the expansion properties can be checked from finite data and give empirical evidence that they hold in practice.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how weak-label errors affect the generalisation of a strong student trained on weak labels, via expansion-based learning theory

open_obligations: Check that Burns et al. actually pose task-level variation in weak-to-strong gain as an open question and that OPEN-1 covers it
Note the citing authors' own limitation that the similarity effect is correlational, not causal
in.other_title: Goel et al. link weak-to-strong gain to low model similarity, addressing a Burns et al. open question
in.rationale: The authors explicitly position their similarity result as a partial answer to an open question raised by Burns et al.; it is a correlational contribution, not a full explanation.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: Why weak-to-strong gains differ across tasks; holds as a correlational finding after controlling for the accuracy gap between the weak supervisor and strong student

text: The authors pose scientific questions including: what explains the relatively strong naive results on NLP datasets versus the poor results with reward models; what makes a concept easy or hard to elicit and how to define salience; whether generalization error can be estimated at test time without labels; how different kinds of weak label errors and biases affect generalization; and how robust the proposed methods are to optimization pressure.
title: Open questions on understanding weak-to-strong generalization and salience
